title: Error Analysis / My Favorite No
subtitle: Students diagnose a common wrong answer — building the concept and practicing it at once, while you see exactly how they’re reasoning.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Leah Alcala, “My Favorite No” (Teaching Channel) · NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Boaler, Mathematical Mindsets (mistakes & brain growth).

blocks.text: What it is
An opener in which the class examines a **wrong answer** and figures out both what the person was thinking *and* where the reasoning went sideways — turning a mistake into the lesson.

**My Favorite No** is a specific, fast version: pose one problem, collect quick responses, and pick a *“favorite no”* — a wrong answer that’s instructive because so many students make it. Celebrate it (“this is my favorite no because it’s so useful”), then the class diagnoses it together. It works because misconceptions don’t disappear when marked wrong; they disappear when *surfaced and reasoned through*.

blocks.title: Why this is the perfect fluency-from-understanding opener

blocks.text: A quiz tells a student `1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5` is wrong and moves on — the misconception survives. Error analysis makes the class confront *why* it’s wrong (you need same-size pieces), so the concept gets built while students practice. And every bit of reasoning is out loud and visible to you.

blocks.text: The routine (My Favorite No)

items: **Pose one problem.** Students solve quickly on a card or whiteboard (e.g., `3/4 − 1/3`).
**Collect & sort.** Gather responses; quickly sort into “yes” and “no” piles without names — this keeps it safe.
**Pick your favorite no.** Choose a wrong answer that reveals a common, instructive misconception. Rewrite it on the board (anonymized).
**Find what’s right first.** “What did this person do that makes sense?” This honors the thinking and lowers the stakes.
**Find where it goes sideways.** “Where does the reasoning break? What would convince this person?” The class reasons to the concept.

blocks.text: Ten minutes, anonymized, and the misconception gets repaired in front of everyone.
What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: “What’s *right* about this thinking?” before “what’s wrong”
Students explaining the misconception, not just “it’s wrong”
The error treated as common and useful, never embarrassing
The concept named by students (“you need the same-size pieces”)
Wrong answers anonymized

no.title: We should not see
items: The student who made the error identified or singled out
“That’s just wrong” with no diagnosis
The teacher explaining the error instead of the class
Moving on the instant the right answer appears
Shaming or laughing at the mistake

blocks.title: The one rule that makes it safe

blocks.text: **Always anonymize the error.** The power of the routine depends on mistakes feeling safe — the moment a student is identified as “the one who got it wrong,” risk-taking dies. Frame every error as a *common, valuable* way of thinking the whole class can learn from.

items: **It reframes mistakes as the path to learning** — powerful for students who have learned to fear being wrong in math, and central to building productive disposition.
**Multilingual learners** benefit from a turn-and-talk (“what do you notice?”) and sentence stems before whole-group diagnosis.
**Diagnosing** rather than producing lets students who are still building confidence engage with the mathematics from a different, lower-pressure angle.
**Honor near-misses:** naming the part of the reasoning that *was* sound tells every student their thinking has value.

blocks.text: Keep a running list of the misconceptions you see most in your unit — those are your best “favorite no’s.” You don’t have to wait for them to appear live; a pre-planned classic error (like adding across on fractions) works just as well.

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson
It’s an **Opener routine** — reach for it when your purpose is to **build a concept while practicing it**, especially around a misconception you know is coming.

Choose Error Analysis over a Number Talk when there’s a specific, predictable error you want to confront head-on (adding fractions across, sign errors, “bigger denominator means bigger fraction”). It pairs naturally with the day’s lesson: diagnose the classic error in the opener, then students carry that corrected understanding into the main task.

Your reflex with a wrong answer is to correct it. Here you do the opposite: you *display* it, protect the student’s anonymity, and ask the class to be the diagnosticians. You’re handing the reasoning to them — which is exactly where the learning is.
Planning one in five minutes

items: **Name the misconception** you want to surface (e.g., “students add numerators and denominators”).
**Pick a problem that triggers it** and write the wrong answer you expect, or collect a real one live.
**Plan the two questions:** “What’s *right* about this thinking?” then “Where does it go sideways — and what would convince this person?”
**Decide your representation** for the fix (a number line, fraction bars, an area model) so the concept becomes visible, not just verbal.

blocks.text: A bank of rational-number errors worth using (6–8)

rows: You must add same-size pieces — need a common denominator.
Direction on the number line; subtracting moves left.
“Of” scales *down* when the factor is less than 1.
Percent of a changing whole — the second 50% is of a smaller amount.

blocks.text: The teacher’s role

yes.title: The teacher does
items: Anonymize and rewrite the error cleanly
Ask “what’s right?” before “what’s wrong?”
Hand the diagnosis to the class
Make the fix visible with a representation
Frame the error as common and useful

no.title: The teacher avoids
items: Naming who made the mistake
Explaining the error for the class
Rushing to “here’s the right way”
Treating it as a gotcha or quiz
**Turn-and-talk first:** “What do you notice about this answer?” lets every student — especially MLLs — rehearse before whole-group.
**Post a stem:** “This makes sense because… but it breaks down when…”
**Use a visual fix** so the concept is accessible without heavy language.

blocks.text: Where this leads

Diagnosing errors trains students to reason about *why* a method works — the exact habit they’ll use in **Core Instruction** when they critique and connect strategies during consolidation. It also builds the classroom norm, central to our vision, that **mistakes are how we learn**.
